#### On-disk Index (v3)

Lore retrieval is fast because Buchbinder maintains an on-disk embedding index at:

```
.opencode/cache/lore-index/index.json
```

The index is built once and reused on every phase invocation. Without the index, `lore-query.mjs` re-embeds every chunk on every call (slow for multi-book series). With the index, query time is O(chunks) cosine comparisons in memory + one local embedding of the query.

**Index coverage** — these source files are scanned:

| Path | Chunked by | Notes |
|------|-----------|-------|
| `series/lorebook/*` | Markdown headings | characters, world, glossary, timeline.json, threads |
| `series/outline.md` | Markdown headings | Cross-book condensed outline (series-level beats) |
| `book/knowledge/*` | Markdown headings | character-profiles, voice-profiles, locations, world-rules, character-voices |
| `book/constitution.md` or `book/manifest.md` | Markdown headings | Project canon/principles — highest priority |
| `book/specification.md` | Markdown headings | Book specification |
| `book/outline.md`, `book/outline/chapter_*.md` | Markdown headings / one-per-file | Whole-book + per-chapter outline |
| `book/drafts/chapter_*.xml` | **XML chunker** (see below) | Drafted chapters |

**Build / refresh the index** — from inside the project:
```bash
# Build or incrementally update the index
node .opencode/lib/scripts/lore-query.mjs --build

# Check status (chunk count, age, embedder version)
node .opencode/lib/scripts/lore-query.mjs --status
```

Or use the slash command: `/buchbinder refresh-index`.

The index build is **incremental**: re-running on an up-to-date index is a no-op. Only source files whose content has changed since the last build are re-chunked and re-embedded. A refresh (see below) rebuilds the index automatically when source files have changed.

**Env overrides.** Retrieval defaults, all overridable:

| Var | Default | Purpose |
|-----|---------|---------|
| `ONNX_EMBED_MODEL` | `Xenova/bge-base-en-v1.5` | ONNX embedding model (768-d) |
| `RERANK_MODEL` | `Xenova/bge-reranker-base` | ONNX cross-encoder |
| `RERANK_BACKEND` | `onnx` | `onnx` \| `none` |
| `CLASSIFIER_MODEL` | `Xenova/nli-deberta-v3-xsmall` | zero-shot / NLI classifier |
| `ONNX_DTYPE` | `q8` | ONNX weight dtype |
| `ONNX_CACHE_DIR` | `~/.cache/buchbinder/models` | shared ONNX model cache |
| `ONNX_OFFLINE` | unset | `1` — never download; use cache or fall back |
| `RERANK_MAX_LENGTH` | `512` | reranker tokenizer truncation length |
| `RERANK_DISABLED` | unset | `1` — force distance-only retrieval |

#### Local ONNX model stack

Three small Transformers.js models power retrieval and quality evidence. They are fetched once into a shared, machine-wide cache and reused by every Buchbinder project:

| Role | Model | ≈Size |
|------|-------|-------|
| Embeddings | `Xenova/bge-base-en-v1.5` | 110 MB |
| Reranking | `Xenova/bge-reranker-base` | 280 MB |
| Classification (NLI) | `Xenova/nli-deberta-v3-xsmall` | 70 MB |

The classifier turns qualitative judgements into local, reproducible evidence — useful for the hard-block quality gates ("does this chapter entail its outline beat?"), the premise stress-test, and non-fiction claim↔source checks:

```bash
# Zero-shot ranking of labels for a passage
node .opencode/lib/classifier.mjs --labels "foreshadowing,pacing,continuity" "the passage text"
# NLI entailment between a premise and a hypothesis
node .opencode/lib/classifier.mjs --entail "Chapter 7 pays off the locket from Chapter 2" "the locket resurfaces"
```

**Wired into the gates.** The classifier runs as a step *inside* two quality gates, chosen because NLI is decisive when a delivered artifact must entail a claimed property: `post-draft` (does the prose entail the draft's own awareness-map claims) and `revision-verify` (does each revision entry entail the critique recommendation it claims to address). Gates whose relation is *correspondence* rather than entailment — such as the outline's setup↔payoff pairing — are deliberately left out, because NLI scores those unreliably and a noisy step erodes gate trust:

```bash
node .opencode/lib/nli-gates.mjs --gate post-draft . --chapter 3
```

Findings are deliberately surgical — lowest entailment first, capped — and persisted to `.opencode/cache/nli-evidence/<gate>.{json,md}` so the evidence is available exactly when the gate runs.

#### Pinned Adjacent Chapters

For draft, critique, and revise phases, the lore query can **pin** specific chapters to be included **verbatim** in the context, regardless of semantic score. This is critical for continuity — the agent drafting chapter N needs the exact last scene of N-1.

```bash
# /buchbinder draft Chapter 5 → include the entire prior chapter (4) verbatim
bun .opencode/lib/scripts/lore-query.mjs \
  --query "Draft context for chapter 5" \
  --pin-chapter 5 --pin-side previous --top 5 --rerank

# /buchbinder critique Chapter 5 → include both N-1 and N+1 verbatim
bun .opencode/lib/scripts/lore-query.mjs \
  --query "Critique context for chapter 5" \
  --pin-chapter 5 --pin-side both --top 5 --rerank
```

- `--pin-side previous` → pin chapter N-1
- `--pin-side next` → pin chapter N+1
- `--pin-side both` → pin both N-1 and N+1

The pinned chapter is loaded from disk directly (bypassing the index). It's emitted in the context block as raw XML, clearly marked as `PINNED — verbatim for continuity`.

#### XML Draft Chunker

`book/drafts/chapter_*.xml` files use a **separate chunker** that understands the draft schema:

```xml
<chapter number="N" title="...">
  <metadata>...</metadata>              <!-- 1 chunk: who/where/when -->
  <awareness-map>
    <sets-up ref="ChM: ...">...</sets-up>
    <payoff-from ref="ChM: ...">...</payoff-from>
    <continuity-anchors>
      <anchor name="...">...</anchor>
    </continuity-anchors>
  </awareness-map>                     <!-- 1 chunk: cross-chapter refs -->
  <scene number="K" type="..." goal="..." conflict="...">
    <narration>...</narration>
    <interiority .../>
    <sensory-inject .../>
  </scene>                              <!-- 1 chunk per <scene> -->
  <scene continuation="true" ...>       <!-- continuation scenes get inferred numbers -->
</chapter>
```

Emits four chunk kinds per file: `metadata`, `awareness`, `scene` (one per `<scene>`), and `whole-chapter` (used only by the pinned path). Continuation scenes (`<scene continuation="true">` with no `number=` attribute) get an inferred sequential number so a 7-scene chapter always produces 7 scene chunks.

The chunker is permissive: missing `<metadata>` or `<awareness-map>` blocks are skipped silently; unknown `<scene>` children are flattened to text. The markdown chunker handles the lore, outline, canon, and spec sources; the XML chunker handles only the drafts.

### Lore as Canonical Truth (Doctrine)

The lorebook — `series/lorebook/*`, `book/knowledge/*`, `book/constitution.md`, `book/specification.md`, and the project `series/outline.md` / `book/outline.md` — is the **absolute source of truth** for a project. Between agents (outline, draft, critique, revise, review), the lorebook is taken as literal, beyond-reproach canon. Only the human user's explicit direction can alter lore; agents must work hard to make internally-consistent sense of canon before suggesting any change.

Why per-project, not an MCP server

Buchbinder is not a server a project connects to; it is a workflow a project *contains*, installed only into that project's own `.opencode/`. That buys granular per-project configuration, no global install or lingering registration, many private projects side by side, and a guided workflow rather than a bare tool surface. Deleting `.opencode/` removes it completely.

### A compound, agentic system

Buchbinder orchestrates LLM inference across a deterministic phase state machine, calls its own typed tools, retrieves from a local embedding index with reranking, evaluates every transition against hard-block gates, and returns control to the author at deliberate checkpoints.

### Built on OpenCode's SDK and plugin surface

Buchbinder registers a project-local TUI plugin (SolidJS + OpenTUI) that renders a custom sidebar, defines keybinds, opens select dialogs, raises toasts, and injects prompts back into the agent. Because the plugin model is native and project-local, the interface ships with the project and cannot rot when a third party stops shipping updates.

### Nix-flake-inspired packaging

Declarative per-project definition, dependency isolation with pinned versions, diff-based non-destructive sync, and override granularity down to individual phase specs.

### On dependencies

Reimplementation is a rational trade when the functionality is small and self-contained, a correct implementation costs minutes to hours, and an LLM can produce it cheaply under review. Buchbinder still uses dependencies where they are genuinely better (`fs-extra`, `fast-xml-parser`, `solid-js`, `@opentui/*`).

## Development

```bash
git clone <repo>
cd buchbinder
node bin/install.mjs --help    # Runs with no node_modules — it self-bootstraps
npm install                    # Only needed to typecheck/build, not to run the installer
npx tsc --noEmit               # Type check
node bin/install.mjs           # Install into the current directory
```

`bin/install.mjs` and `bin/refresh.mjs` are three-line launchers: they call
`ensureDeps()` (`bin/lib/bootstrap.mjs`) and then dynamically import the real
CLI body (`bin/lib/install.mjs`, `bin/lib/refresh.mjs`). That
indirection is what lets the bin run from a bare clone — the third-party
imports (`chalk`, `fs-extra`, `@inquirer/prompts`) are only resolved *after*
the dependencies they need have been installed.

Source structure:
- `src/commands/buchbinder-router.md` — Hub phase router (direct `/buchbinder-router <phase>`)
- `src/tools/hubs/buchbinder/` — 29 subcommand spec files
- `src/lib/` — 32 library files (gates, voice, checkpoints, analyses, etc.)
- `src/skills/` — 34 SKILL.md files across 5 categories
- `src/templates/` — Track templates (fiction, non-fiction, series)
- `bin/install.mjs`, `bin/refresh.mjs` — self-bootstrapping launchers (call `ensureDeps()`, then load the CLI body)
- `bin/lib/bootstrap.mjs` — resolves/installs the package's own runtime deps so the bins run from a bare clone
- `bin/lib/install.mjs`, `bin/lib/refresh.mjs` — the installer / refresher bodies

## OpenCode v2 migration

Buchbinder's TUI integration and command dispatch were migrated to the **OpenCode v2** plugin/command model and kept fully **self-contained** (project-local):

- **Server hooks**: `src/hooks-plugin/` exports a v2 server plugin (`id` + `setup(ctx)`) and is installed to `.opencode/plugins/hooks/`.
- **TUI sidebar/menu**: `src/plugins/buchbinder-sidebar.tsx` uses `@opencode/plugin/tui` (`Plugin.define`, `setup`, `ui.router/dialog/toast/slot`, `keymap.layer`). A single `/buchbinder` slash entry opens the phase menu; `/buchbinder <phase> [details]` dispatches directly. Menu selection and phase shortcuts open a details/instructions prompt (Enter to run, Esc to cancel), so users can add context without memorizing subcommands.
- **Clickable sidebar shortcuts**: Sidebar menu items are interactive shortcuts — the title/footer "Open Buchbinder Menu" action and Dashboard quick actions open the same `/buchbinder` popup menu or phase details/dispatch flow as menu selection (not raw prompt staging), enabling one-click entry with popup details.
- **Session-aware dispatch**: prompts are submitted (not merely staged) via the v2 session prompt API. If no session is active, the sidebar creates one and navigates to it before submission, avoiding "open a session first" dead ends and surfacing failures via toast.
- **Self-contained routing**: Buchbinder phases never call `hubMenu` and never route to global/user-scope OpenCode hubs. The project-local router/specs (`src/tools/buchbinder-router.ts`, `src/tools/hubs/buchbinder/*.ts`) and guarded dispatch instruct the agent to use this project's installed `.opencode/` skills, commands, and tools only.
- **Install/refresh (v2, idempotent)**: `bin/lib/sync.mjs`, `install.mjs`, and `refresh.mjs` copy hooks + sidebar + skills + tools + commands + templates + rules, normalize legacy config, and register local plugins in project `opencode.jsonc` via the v2 `plugins` key. `tui.json` is kept minimal/clean of misplaced plugin registration; plugin discovery/registration is project-local. `refresh --force` overwrites plugin-owned drift and rebuilds the install manifest in one pass (idempotent reruns are no-ops when up to date).
- **Dispatcher removed:** the legacy `src/commands/buchbinder.md` text dispatcher is removed. The `/buchbinder` entrypoint is the plugin menu (picker + per-subcommand palette/slash entries), backed by registered project subcommands (e.g. `buchbinder-gates`, `buchbinder-router`, `buchbinder-split-outline`) and installed skills/tools.
- **Project config:** `.opencode.json` / `opencode.jsonc` register project-local plugins; install/refresh/sync keep plugins, commands, skills, tools, rules, templates, and manifests in sync per project.

## What Buchbinder Adds

While the DNA of the eight-step fiction methodology originates from the projects above, Buchbinder introduces substantial new architecture, binding, and tooling:

| Area | Novelty |
|------|---------|
| **Non-fiction track** | Full non-fiction workflow with thesis/argument structuring, citation management (APA, Chicago, MLA, IEEE), source evaluation, and bibliography generation — no antecedent exists in either source project. |
| **Research phase** | Active research ingestion: web search integration, source extraction and annotation, interview methods, field notes, and literature review workflows. The original treated research as passive genre knowledge only. |
| **Critique workflow** | 8 structured critique modes (alpha, beta, peer, sensitivity, cold-read, comprehensive, adversarial two-agent dialectic, personas with 3-5 reader types) as a distinct phase with feedback categorization and prioritization matrices. The original had only self-editing. |
| **Revision cycle** | Dedicated revision planning between critique and edit with a revision-verify gate, plus `--depth full` multi-pass revision (structural→language→pacing). The original looped directly from review back to edit. |
| **Three-pass editing** | Line-edit (craft) → copy-edit (mechanics) → proofread (typos) as distinct passes, each with a different focus. |
| **Publish pipeline** | Pandoc-integrated multi-format export with post-export verification, replacing Fiction Fabricator's direct Python generators. |
| **25 hard-block quality gates** | Evidence-based pass/fail gates across 7 categories (outline, pre-draft, post-draft, revision, structural, linguistic, experience). No soft warnings — gates block progression on failure. No antecedent had programmatic quality gates. |
| **Fine-grained outline with gate** | Scene beats (min 2/chapter), setup/payoff bidirectionality, continuity anchors, pacing distribution — with a quality gate that blocks drafting if the outline is too coarse, plus 3 revision cycles. |
| **Awareness maps** | Each chapter loads only its outline slice (scene beats, payoff-from, sets-up, continuity anchors, adjacent summaries) instead of the whole book. Post-draft gate verifies the awareness map was honored. |
| **Phase 2 structural analyses** | 14 dedicated analysis libraries: reverse outline, character arc, Q/A accounting, promise audit, escalation curve, subtext, rhythm, purple prose, immersion, trust, cognitive load, knowledge state, opening/closing, cliché detection. |
| **Voice fingerprinting** | Per-character AND per-narration voice profiles with independent fingerprints. |
| **Modular style sheets** | 5 separate modules (prose, dialogue, description, pacing, POV) instead of a monolithic style document. |
| **Series lorebook** | Cross-book knowledge base with inheritance, sync, audit, and external import (SillyTavern/JanitorAI/CharacterAI). |
| **Premise stress-test** | 6-criteria hard block before specification begins. |
| **Thematic statement** | Required, testable argument (not just a topic) in the constitution, referenced by outline and critique. |
| **TypeScript tooling** | All internal tools written in TypeScript — 26 spec files, 32 library files, compiled via OpenCode's JIT tool loading. The original used Python only. |
| **Per-project plugin** | Designed specifically for per-book `.opencode/` installation as an npm-installable plugin, not a global resource. |
| **Command architecture** | `/buchbinder` hub with 25 subcommands via `hubMenu` routing rather than flat top-level commands. Full project state machine with phase detection, drift analysis, and contextual navigation. |
| **Batch-first defaults** | All pipeline phases default to batch processing (up to 6 chapters) with shared context loaded once per batch. Single-chapter is an explicit override. |
| **Serious tone** | Professional register throughout — no emoji in command output, no tutorial-style cheerful framing. |

OpenCode's TUI provides three sidebar slots that plugins can render into:

**Plugin type**: `TuiPluginModule` (from `@opencode-ai/plugin/tui`)

## Key Design Decisions

1. **Direct lib calls, not API** — The sidebar calls Buchbinder's 40 lib files directly as functions. No HTTP API, no subprocess. Fast, type-safe, no network overhead.

2. **Agent ops via prompt injection** — When the author clicks "Start Phase", the sidebar injects `/buchbinder draft` into OpenCode's prompt via `api.client.tui.appendPrompt()`. OpenCode's agent handles the actual drafting. This reuses the existing 26 specs without reimplementation.

3. **SolidJS signals for reactivity** — `createSignal()` for tab state, gate results, diff hunks. When a gate runs or a hunk is approved, the signal updates and the UI re-renders instantly.

4. **Box-drawing charts** — All visualizations use Unicode box-drawing characters (╱ ╲ ╴ ╵ █ ░ ▌ ▐) with ANSI colors from `api.theme.current`. No external chart library — the terminal is the canvas.

5. **4 tabs, not 8 panels** — The 8 HITL features are grouped into 4 tabs by function: Dashboard (phase preview, intent, provenance), Gates (all 26 gates), Diff (diff approval, veto, feedback memory), Viz (visualizations). This keeps the sidebar focused.

6. **Veto key (`|`) works everywhere** — In any tab, pressing `|` opens the veto input for the currently focused suggestion (gate, hunk, or critique item).

# Buchbinder — Expansion Plan

## Problem Statement
How might we expand Buchbinder's pipeline so that each phase produces measurably better output, quality is enforced at every transition, and the system handles the realities of long-form AI-assisted writing — voice drift, continuity breaks, context loss, and unverified revisions — while delivering a full publication suite with series support?

## Recommended Direction

Build in three layers, each layer making the previous one better:

### Layer 1: Verified Quality Pipeline (Foundation)
The pipeline enforces quality at every phase transition. No phase can be skipped without explicit override. Every checklist item is verified, not just checked off. The critique→revise loop becomes a verified cycle. Voice drift is detected automatically. Context persists across sessions via checkpoints.

**New subcommands:**
- `/buchbinder verify` — Run quality gate for current phase (prerequisites, output completeness, continuity)
- `/buchbinder resume` — Load checkpoint, reconstruct context efficiently for mid-chapter continuation

**Enhanced existing phases:**
- `draft` — Pre-draft gate verifies all 13 context items loaded (produces evidence, not just "checked"). Post-draft gate verifies tracking updated, chapter meets outline purpose. Voice check against voice profile (generated after chapter 3).
- `critique` — Adds verification that critique items are specific enough to be actionable (not "this could be better" but "paragraph 3, the motivation is unclear")
- `revise` — Adds revision verification: cross-reference critique items against revision log, report unaddressed critical/major items, block progression if critical items remain
- `edit` — Checks against style sheet (living document of every style/terminology decision)
- `review` — Runs automated continuity scan (character states, timeline, plot threads, terminology) across all chapters

**New artifacts:**
- `./book/knowledge/voice-profile.md` — Generated after chapter 3, maintained as chapters are added. Captures: sentence length distribution, dialogue-to-prose ratio, sensory detail density, character-specific speech patterns, emotional register.
- `./book/style-sheet.md` — Living document. Every phase that makes a style or continuity decision appends to it. Edit phase checks against it. Review validates it.
- `./book/checkpoints/chapter-N.json` — Context state after each chapter. Records what was loaded, what changed, what needs to be loaded next time.

### Layer 2: Per-Chapter Editorial Cycle + Real Publishing
After infrastructure setup, each chapter goes through its own complete editorial cycle. Publishing uses real pandoc integration. New quality sub-phases add professional editorial depth.

**New subcommands:**
- `/buchbinder cycle Chapter N` — Runs full editorial cycle for one chapter: draft → critique → revise → edit → continuity-check → mark done
- `/buchbinder pacing-audit` — Analyze pacing distribution across all chapters, identify saggy sections
- `/buchbinder hook-review` — Check each chapter's opening/closing hooks
- `/buchbinder read-through` — Full read-through as a reader (not editor), flag confusion/engagement drops

**Enhanced `publish` phase:**
- Detect and integrate with pandoc (the universal document converter)
- `publish-config.json` — format preferences, cover image, metadata, pandoc options
- Actual EPUB 3 / DOCX / LaTeX / PDF / HTML output via pandoc
- Post-export verification (EPUB validates, DOCX opens, file sizes reasonable)
- Fallback: manual generation if pandoc not available (with warning)

**Enhanced task tracking:**
- Per-chapter status: each chapter has its own `draft → critique → revise → edit → done` lifecycle
- `tasks.md` gains per-chapter sub-status, not just global phase status

### Layer 3: Series Infrastructure
Multi-book support. Knowledge bases that persist across books. Series-level tracking.

**New structure:**
- `./series/bible/` — Cross-book knowledge base (character profiles, world-setting, glossary)
- `./series/timeline.json` — Series-level timeline spanning all books
- `track.json` gains `seriesId` and `bookNumber` fields
- `constitute` for book 2+ offers "inherit from series bible" option

## Key Assumptions to Validate
- [ ] The agent can produce **evidence-based verification** (not just "checked" but "here's what I found"). Test: run a draft gate and see if it reports specific findings or just says "all good."
- [ ] Voice profile comparison actually catches drift. Test: deliberately write chapter 5 in a different voice and see if the check flags it.
- [ ] Checkpoint/resume actually saves context loading time. Test: resume chapter 10 and measure how many files are loaded vs. cold start.
- [ ] Pandoc is available or installable on the target system. Test: `which pandoc` on the user's machine.

# XML Chapter Structure for Buchbinder

The XML layer is an **intermediate representation** — the agent generates chapters with internal XML tags for verification, error recovery, and element extraction. XML tags are **stripped on save** to produce clean prose. The agent uses them during generation to maintain focus, and the quality gates parse them to verify content against project standards.

## Save Transformation

On save, the agent:
1. Strips all XML tags
2. Replaces `<dialogue speaker="X">text</dialogue>` with `"text"` (preserving the text, adding dialogue punctuation)
3. Replaces `<narration>text</narration>` with `text` (raw prose)
4. Replaces `<exposition>text</exposition>` with `text`
5. Converts `<chapter-notes>` to the footer notes section
6. Saves clean prose to `./book/content/chapter_NNNNN.md`
7. Saves the XML version to `./book/drafts/chapter_NNNNN.xml` (for verification gates)

## Quality Gate Integration

The quality gates parse the XML version, not the clean prose. This allows:
- **Pre-draft gate**: Verify `<metadata>` matches outline (chapter number, title, pacing tag, characters present)
- **Post-draft gate**: Verify `<chapter-notes>` tracking updates match tracking files, word count met, hooks present
- **Voice check**: Extract all `<dialogue speaker="X">` blocks, compare against X's voice profile. Extract all `<narration register="Y">` blocks, compare against narration voice profile.
- **Continuity check**: Extract `<tracking-updates>`, cross-reference against tracking files. Extract `<beatchange>` sequences, verify emotional arc makes sense.
- **Citation check (non-fiction)**: Extract all `<evidence>` and `<citation>` tags, verify sources exist, pages valid, format correct.
- **Revision verify**: After revise, parse XML to confirm critique items were addressed (e.g., if critique said "character motivation unclear in scene 2", verify scene 2 was modified)

## What this does

1. Loads the project root (cwd)

## When to use

- You want a quick health check without going through the full `/buchbinder verify` flow
- You just finished a revision and want to see the new gate state
- The sidebar's "Run All Gates" button is what you want, but you're in the prompt, not the sidebar

## Implementation

The agent calls the buchbinder lib directly:

```typescript
import { runGate } from './tools/quality-gates.js'
import { detectState } from './tools/project-state.js'

const state = detectState(projectRoot)
const gates = ['outline', 'pre-draft', 'post-draft', 'revision-verify', 'continuity-check', 'non-negotiables']
for (const id of gates) {
  const r = runGate(id, projectRoot)
  // print r.status, r.blocking, r.warnings
}
```

Or via the **Run All Gates** button in the sidebar.

The AI-writing tell scan (word tiers, structural tells, signature slop) is part of the post-draft and review gates — see `rules/ai-writing-patterns.md` and `skills/quality-assurance/ai-writing-audit/`. Any P0 (credibility killer) pattern blocks.

There is no global keybind. Single-letter bindings would block typing, modifier+letter pairs collide with OpenCode's built-ins, and leader-based bindings require expansion that wasn't worth the complexity. Use the button or the slash command.

# Buchbinder — AI-Writing Pattern Rule

## MANDATORY RULE

Every prose phase — **draft, critique, revise, edit, review, verify** — must apply the AI-writing pattern catalog. The method is `skills/quality-assurance/ai-writing-audit/SKILL.md`; the catalog is `skills/quality-assurance/ai-writing-audit/references/patterns.md`. Load the skill before any prose pass that writes, judges, or repairs prose.

This rule is the standing constraint. Where a phase's gate is stricter, the gate wins; this rule is the floor.

## Signals, not proof

The patterns are statistically more common in LLM output, but humans on autopilot — under deadline pressure, in unfamiliar genres, or in a second language — produce the same shapes. Independent audits put detector false-positive rates above 60% on non-native English writers.

Treat a flag as **signal, not verdict**. Never use pattern density as the sole basis for a consequential decision (publication, attribution, a verdict on who wrote a passage). Report the flag and the reason; let the author decide.

## The three tiers

Full lists in the catalog. In short:

- **Tier 1 — review every match.** 1A = AI frequency markers (`delve`, `leverage`, `tapestry`, `testament to`, `robust`, …) — evidence about how a passage was produced. 1B = clarity edits (`utilize`, `in order to`, `serves as`, …) — good writing regardless of who wrote it, **not** authorship evidence.
- **Tier 2 — flag when 2+ appear in the same paragraph.** (`harness`, `navigate`, `foster`, `crucial`, `nuanced`, `ecosystem`, …). One isolated occurrence is never a finding.
- **Tier 3 — flag by density.** A common word (`significant`, `innovative`, `effective`, …) only when that one word alone hits `max(3, floor(wordCount × 0.03))` uses.
- **Tier 3 phrases** — a boilerplate phrase repeated 2+ times, or 3+ distinct phrases in one piece.

## Severity

- **P0 — credibility killers.** Cutoff disclaimers, chatbot artifacts ("I hope this helps"), vague attributions ("experts believe"), significance inflation on routine events.
- **P1 — obvious AI smell.** Word-list violations, template phrases, "Let's" openers, synonym cycling, formulaic openings, hedge-stacked predictions, invented contrast pairs, bullet lists of bare noun phrases.
- **P2 — stylistic polish.** Em-dash frequency, generic conclusions, copula avoidance, transition phrases, uniform paragraph length, repeated punchlines.

Map to the Buchbinder severity tiers: P0 → Critical, P1 → Major, P2 → Minor.

## Never inject (rewrite-side failures)

A rewrite fails even when it scores clean if it **adds** any of these:

- **Fabricated speaker perspective** — "I've seen this a hundred times" with no source support.
- **Manufactured stakes** — "now more than ever," "the stakes have never been higher."
- **Forced contrarianism** — "everyone says X, but they're wrong."
- **Performed candor** — "let's be honest," "real talk."
- **Em-dash theatrics** — dashes added for drama the content has not earned.
- **Staccato conversion** — chopping ordinary sentences into fragments to manufacture rhythm.
- **Invented specifics** — an unsupported number, name, date, or mechanism. A fabricated specific is worse than the vague phrasing it replaced.

Subtract and sharpen. Never invent.

## Fiction carve-outs

The catalog is calibrated for English prose broadly. Fiction is explicitly exempt where the device is the point: manufactured punchlines, staccato drama, fragments, anaphora, and deliberate repetition pass when they carry voice, comedy, or tension. Judge the *function*, not the shape — an earned fragment is craft; a run of same-shape fragments posing as reveals is a tell.

## Where it binds

| Phase | Application |
|-------|-------------|
| **draft** | Prevention — write in the style key and the good-prose qualities; do not inject the never-inject list. Post-draft gate scans for the worst patterns. |
| **critique** | Detection — the Anti-AI-Slop mandate runs in every mode; word tiers and structural tells are reported as findings. |
| **revise** | Repair — fix flagged patterns while preserving meaning, attribution, and the author's voice. |
| **edit** | Line-edit pass runs the full catalog as a hard-block gate; never-inject guardrails bound every suggestion. |
| **review** | Project-wide gate — AI-tell density is a publication-readiness check. |
| **verify** | On-demand audit — report the tier findings without rewriting. |

The Buchbinder system MUST be completely self-contained within each project's `.opencode/` directory. Under NO circumstances may any part of the system be installed to, registered in, or reference:

- `~/.config/opencode/tui.json`
- `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`
- `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`
- `~/.config/opencode/agents/`
- `~/.config/opencode/skills/`
- `~/.config/opencode/rules/`
- `~/.config/opencode/commands/`

## What This Means in Practice

1. **Never add the buchbinder-sidebar plugin to `~/.config/opencode/tui.json`**
2. **Never copy plugin files to `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`**
3. **Never suggest adding anything to global config as a "fix"**
4. **Never install dependencies in `~/.config/opencode/node_modules/`**
5. **Never register commands, skills, agents, or rules globally**

## Correct Installation Target

ALL files go to `<project>/.opencode/`:

| Asset | Destination |
|-------|-------------|
| Plugin (TUI) | `.opencode/plugins/buchbinder-sidebar/` |
| Plugin (hooks) | `.opencode/plugins/hooks/` |

| Tools | `.opencode/tools/` |

## Why

This system must work identically when installed via `node bin/install.mjs` on any machine, for any user, without requiring any changes to their global OpenCode configuration. The install script (`bin/install.mjs`) is the sole mechanism for provisioning — it copies everything into the project's `.opencode/` and registers plugins in `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` and `.opencode/tui.json` (both project-local).

## Pattern catalog

Grouped. Each entry names the tell and the fix.

### Sentence and structure

- **Negative parallelism** — "It's not X — it's Y." Flags only when a second frame starts within three sentences. Fix: state the positive claim directly.
- **Negation chains** — two or more "no …" items in a row ("No fluff, no filler, no jargon"). Fix: say what the thing *is*. One negation earns its place; a chain is a drumroll.
- **Same-opener sentence runs** — three or more consecutive sentences opening on the same word, unless the anaphora does persuasive work. Pronoun-opener runs are ordinary narration.
- **Stranded auxiliary contrast** — "The tool died; the data didn't." Ration to one; write the next contrast out in full.
- **Colon into a triple** — a colon opening onto exactly three comma-separated items. Audit the list; weigh by genre.
- **Manufactured punchlines / staccato drama** — three or more same-shape fragments in a row, each posing as a reveal. **Fiction carve-out:** keep fragments that carry voice or tension; fold the rest into ordinary sentences.
- **Aphorism formulas** — "X is the language of Y," "the architecture of trust," "X is not a tool but a mirror." Replace with the source-supported claim. Quotations and established idioms pass.
- **Excessive structure** — more than 3 headings in under 300 words; 8+ bullets in under 200; formulaic headers ("Overview," "Key Points"). Merge or rename only when structural editing is authorized.
- **Inline-header lists** — bullets where each item repeats its bold header ("**Performance:** Performance improved by…"). Strip the redundant label.
- **List-label periods** — a short bold noun-phrase label followed by a period then a gloss. Use a colon and lowercase the gloss.

### Inflation and significance

- **Significance inflation** — "marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of…", "a watershed moment for the industry." Delete the inflation clause if the sentence still works.
- **Novelty inflation** — "introduced a term," "coined the phrase," "a failure mode nobody talks about." Remove the unsupported novelty claim; describe the supported action.
- **"Real/actual" adjective inflation** — "real on-chain tokenomics," "genuine utility." Drop the adjective unless the sentence names the fake version.
- **Moral-adjective category errors** — "an honest shape," "flagged honestly." Cut the unsupported moral adjective; state a concrete property.
- **Generic future-narrative closers** — modal + "become" + "the most [adjective] (narrative/trend/chapter)." Use a falsifiable version only when the source supplies it.
- **Generic conclusions** — "The future looks bright," "Only time will tell," "As we move forward." Cut; add a closer only when the source supplies one.

### Hedging and confidence

- **Hedge-stacked predictions** — "could potentially," "may eventually unlock." Keep the one qualifier that retains the intended uncertainty.
- **Confidence calibration phrases** — "It's worth noting that," "Interestingly," "Notably," "Undeniably." Flag by density; let the fact speak.
- **Parenthetical hedging** — "(and, increasingly, Z)," "(or, more precisely, Y)." Give the aside its own sentence or cut it.
- **False concession structure** — "While X is impressive, Y remains a challenge." Make the concession specific or cut the frame.

### Voice and stance

- **Chatbot artifacts** — "I hope this helps!", "Certainly!", "Great question!" Remove entirely.
- **Sycophantic tone** — "Excellent point!", "You're absolutely right!" Remove.
- **"Let's" constructions** — "Let's explore," "Let's break this down." Start with the point.
- **Narrated candor** — "I want to be upfront:", "To be fully transparent:" Cut the frame; keep the disclosure. **Carve-out:** substantive admissions and conflict-of-interest disclosures stay.
- **Acknowledgment loops** — "You're asking about…", "To answer your question…" Just answer. **Carve-out:** a reply that orients the reader to which question is being answered.
- **Performed-insight phrases** — "sit with that for a moment," "that's not nothing," "the part nobody mentions," "X is dead; long live X," sentence-initial "Turns out." One is style; several is a tell.
- **Stock reaction framing** — "What surprised me most," "I was fascinated to discover." Keep authentic, specific reactions.
- **Lingering-attention claims** — "the line I keep coming back to," "I can't stop thinking about this." **Carve-out:** a reason attached.
- **Self-labeling significance** — "That last move is the contrarian one." Cut the label; let the description carry the weight.
- **Infomercial engagement hooks** — "The catch?", "Here's the thing.", "Plot twist:". Delete the hook and state the thing.
- **Dramatized contrast against the crowd** — "shipped it in 2022, while everyone else was still debating timelines." Cut the crowd clause; name a competitor only when the source does.

### Attribution and evidence

- **Vague attributions** — "Experts believe," "Studies show," "Research suggests." Cite the source or cut the claim.
- **Vague third-party validation** — "independent testing confirms," "analysts agree." Name the source, test, and result, or cut.
- **Notability name-dropping** — a stack of prestigious citations that borrows weight without showing why each matters. One supported reference beats four name-drops.
- **Superficial -ing analyses** — strings of participles as pseudo-analysis: "symbolizing the region's commitment, reflecting decades of investment." Replace with facts or cut.
- **Promotional language** — "nestled within the breathtaking foothills," "a vibrant hub of innovation." Use a plain description or cut.
- **Formulaic challenges** — "Despite challenges, [subject] continues to thrive." Name the challenge and response, or cut.
- **Speculative gap-filling** — "is believed to have," "likely began his career in." Cut the speculation; use a supplied fact.

### Specificity and concreteness

- **False ranges** — "from the Big Bang to dark matter." List the actual topics.
- **Transformation crutch** — repeated unexplained relabeling ("the concern turns into panic"). Ask what changed; use supplied facts. Literal transformations pass.
- **False agency** — "The decision emerged after the offsite." Name the actor only when the source identifies them.
- **Copula avoidance** — "serves as," "features," "boasts." Default to "is" or "has" unless a more specific verb adds meaning.
- **Synonym cycling** — "developers… engineers… practitioners… builders" for the same referent. Use the clearest term consistently.
- **Bullet lists of bare noun phrases** — 5+ consecutive ≤6-word adjective-plus-noun items with no verb. Convert to prose or full claims only when authorized. Genuine list content (changelogs, parameter docs) passes.
- **Unfilled placeholders** — `[Your Name]`, `[INSERT SOURCE]`, `2025-XX-XX`. Fill with supplied content or flag the gap.
- **Cutoff disclaimers** — "As of my last update," "While specific details are limited." Remove; never turn missing information into a confident claim.
- **AI-tool URL parameters / citation-markup leaks** — `utm_source=chatgpt.com`, `citeturn0search0`, `contentReference[oaicite:0]`. Strip the token; the presence is the signature.

### Rhythm and uniformity

- **Uniform sentence length** — a run of similarly shaped sentences. Vary by clarifying, not by imposing word-count bands.
- **Uniform paragraph length** — repeated same-size paragraphs whose boundaries do not follow the argument. Keep regular structure when the genre calls for it.
- **Em-dash frequency** — above 1 per 1,000 words. Writing-quality guidance, **not** evidence of machine authorship.
- **Suspiciously clean grammar** — don't sand away deliberate fragments, sentences starting with "And"/"But", or comma splices for effect.
- **Read-aloud test** — if the text could pass through TTS without sounding odd, it is probably too uniform.
- **Treadmill effect** — could you cut 40–60% and lose no information? Report during cleanup; condense only when authorized.
- **Paragraph-reshuffle immunity** — if you can swap two body paragraphs without breaking the piece, it is a list, not an argument.

`linkedin` · `blog` (default, full strength) · `technical-blog` · `investor-email` (tightest) · `docs` · `casual` (worst offenders only).

Ornamental uses and `delve`/`tapestry`/`beacon`/`embark`/`testament to`/`game-changer` still flag.

## Voice profiles

Optional and independent of context. Infer from the source's existing register; never impose a persona on text that already has one. Bounded by the never-inject list.

- **`casual`** — contractions, direct conversational sentences; no forced fragments or length quota.
- **`professional`** — active voice where the actor matters; concrete claims when supplied; never invent a source behind "experts say."
- **`technical`** — plain copulatives ("X is Y") over "serves as"/"stands as a testament to"; preserve accurate technical terms.
- **`warm`** — address the reader where the source already does; cut empty intensifiers; avoid performative-empathy openers.
- **`blunt`** — lead with the claim; rare em-dashes; cut hedge stacks but preserve modals that carry uncertainty.

**Calibrate to a sample:** given a sample of the author's own prose, match its sentence-length pattern, contraction rate, paragraph openings, and recurring word choices instead of a named profile. Don't "upgrade" the vocabulary.

## Fiction note

The catalog is calibrated for English prose broadly. Fiction is exempt where the device is the point: manufactured punchlines, staccato drama, fragments, anaphora, and deliberate repetition pass when they carry voice, comedy, or tension. The never-inject list still applies — a rewrite must not add a fragment run, a manufactured stake, or an invented specific the author did not write.

# 76 Authors Variation 


This list of AI generated retellings of the same blurb from the Snow White story is intended as a quick reference for indiivuduals to compare narrative voices quickly in the context of asking an LLM to generate text in a specific style or blend thereof.

# Good English Prose — Qualities to Write Toward

The qualities below separate strong prose from output that is merely correct. They are the **positive counterpart** to [`../bot-slop.md`](../bot-slop.md): that guide catalogs what to remove, this one names what to build. The list is reproduced as given.

**Where this is used**

- **The model's output** — compressed into the always-on `@Prose Craft` directive in the preset ([Presets and Prompts](../presets-guide.md)), so every reply is written toward them.
- **Greetings** — the greeting is the most-copied text on the card, so it is written and scored against them ([First Message and Alternate Greetings](../character-card/greetings.md)).
- **Verification** — prose quality is a scored dimension ([Verification](../character-card/verification.md) §1.2, dimension 11).
- **Every prose field** — [Description](../character-card/description.md), [Personality](../character-card/personality.md), [Scenario](../character-card/scenario.md), [Example Dialogues](../character-card/example-dialogues.md), [System Prompt](../character-card/system-prompt.md), [Post-History Instructions](../character-card/post-history-instructions.md).
- **The player's own posts** — [Roleplay Technique](../roleplay-guide.md) §1.

---

## The qualities

1. **Control of voice** — the narration has a consistent, identifiable sensibility, and that voice is doing work beyond decoration: it carries judgment, mood, and meaning the way sound carries a song.
2. **Sentences with varied cadence** — rhythm alternates between long and short, latinate and plain, so paragraphs breathe. Monotone sentence length is the most common tell of weak prose no matter how correct the grammar.
3. **Precision of word choice** — the right noun and verb instead of an adverb patching up a lazy one. The revision instinct is to cut modifiers, not add them.
4. **Concreteness over abstraction** — emotional states are rendered as physical, sensory, situational fact rather than named. "Grief" is a cold cup of tea she doesn't drink, not "she felt profound grief."
5. **The five senses deployed unevenly and pointedly** — smell and touch often neglected by amateurs; the best work uses them precisely and sparingly, so a sensory detail registers as information rather than texture for its own sake.
6. **Subtext** — characters say approximately what they mean, and the gap between their words and their situation is where the scene lives. Dialogue carries the load of what is left unsaid.
7. **Dialogue that is distinct per speaker** — you could remove the attribution tags and still know who is talking, because vocabulary, syntax, rhythm, and evasions are individuated.
8. **Resistance to exposition** — backstory arrives through objects, actions, textures, and misdirected remarks; the dump is displaced or dissolved. Information is rationed and earned.
9. **Structural architecture** — the plot is load-bearing: every scene changes the situation, and the arrangement of chapters (chronology, framing, braiding, withheld knowledge) is itself meaningful.
10. **Momentum and causality** — events follow from character rather than from authorial convenience; coincidence may open a door but never solve the problem.
11. **A living, specific world** — place is rendered with local particularity: weather, economy, speech, food, labor, hierarchy. The setting could not be swapped into another novel without loss.
12. **Characters with interior contradiction** — people want incompatible things, act against their stated values, and are capable of surprising the reader without becoming implausible.
13. **Moral seriousness** — the novel engages stakes larger than personal satisfaction, and the author's intelligence shows in how tensions are held open rather than resolved glibly.
14. **Themes enacted, not announced** — the meaning emerges from the arrangement of events and images, not from a character stepping forward to state the point. No thesis sentences doing the theme's work.
15. **Imagery that recurs and mutates** — a motif (a scar, a river, a debt) returns changed at each appearance, accumulating meaning across the whole book.
16. **Inevitability and surprise together** — the ending feels both unexpected and unsurpassable, the way a good joke's punchline is. Retrospectively, it was always the only ending.
17. **Compression and restraint** — the best passages omit whatever can be inferred; the reader is trusted to assemble meaning, and the omitted thing is often the emotional center.
18. **Tonal coherence** — even a book spanning comedy and horror has a governing tone that unifies shifts rather than whipsawing the reader arbitrarily.
19. **Show-then-trust pacing** — the writer establishes a pattern, then violates it meaningfully; setups are paid off (or deliberately refused) with awareness of the expectation created.
20. **Revision visible as polish** — paragraphs are irreducible: try to cut one sentence and something is lost. This is the fingerprint of many drafts.
21. **Physical and psychological accuracy** — biology, craft, labor, and psychology behave as they actually do, which is what lets the reader suspend disbelief elsewhere.
22. **Point of view used as a tool** — the chosen lens (first, close third, omniscient, unreliable) is exploited for what only it can do, not merely defaulted to.
23. **Tension sustained at the level of the sentence** — even quiet domestic scenes hold pressure because the reader knows something is at stake or feels something is being withheld.
24. **Restrained, non-adjectival emotion** — the cataclysmic moments are frequently the calmest in register, which produces more feeling than escalation would.
25. **Immersive interiority, but not solipsism** — access to a character's mind deepens rather than narrows the world; their consciousness is a window, not a cell.
26. **Avoidance of stock constructions** — clichés, reflexive similes, sententious summary, and filler are ruthlessly excised, because the writer hears where the reader's eye will glide past.
27. **Narrative generosity** — the book gives the reader something to feel, think, and argue about; it does not merely perform its own cleverness.
28. **Originality of angle** — even a familiar story is told from an unexpected aperture: a perspective, a form, a structure, a moral premise not seen before in that combination.
29. **The ending earns its weight** — resolution is proportionate to the promises made, and ambiguity, when used, is controlled rather than evasive.
30. **A felt sense of obsession** — the writer was clearly trying to solve something that mattered to them, and that pressure is legible on every page.

---

## Working with the list

The qualities are a direction, not a checklist to recite. Two notes on applying them:

- **They are the positive form of the slop rules.** Where [`bot-slop.md`](../bot-slop.md) names a construction to cut, a quality here names the habit to build in its place. Concrete-over-abstraction (4) is the fix for "she felt profound grief"; avoidance of stock constructions (26) is the fix for the catalogued clichés; restrained emotion (24) is the fix for melodrama.
- **A scene is judged on the whole.** No single quality is a pass/fail gate on its own. The test is whether the passage would lose something if a sentence were cut (20), whether the voice could belong to another card (1, 7), and whether the reader is trusted to assemble meaning (17).

## Alternative Thoughts

- **The list as a generation prompt.** Feeding all thirty qualities verbatim to the model each turn produces purple prose and self-consciousness; the preset compresses them into a short directive instead. The full list is for the human writing and reviewing, not for pasting.
- **Treating them as a rubric.** Scoring prose against thirty dimensions is slow and noisy. The guides use a small number of scored dimensions (register, prose quality) and hold the rest as direction.

## Common premise failures

# Antagonist Design

The antagonist is the story's embodied **counter-argument**: the character who believes and acts on the counter-premise (see `controlling-idea.md`). Scenes trade wins between the two positions until the climax delivers the verdict. Design the antagonist to deserve that role.

The antagonist must be stronger than the protagonist in at least one dimension — intelligence, resources, position, ruthlessness, or conviction. A weaker antagonist makes the protagonist's victory feel unearned and the theme's verdict feel rigged. No one is the villain of their own story. The antagonist acts on a coherent moral logic — the counter-premise stated as something a person could defend:

- Not "I want power because I am evil" but "Order requires a strong hand; mercy is weakness that gets people killed."

# The Controlling Idea

Robert McKee's *Story* frames a story's theme as a **controlling idea**: a value plus its cause, stated as one sentence — e.g. "Justice triumphs because the hero is smarter than the criminals" (paraphrased concept). Theme *words* ("justice", "redemption") can't guide a scene decision; a controlling idea can, because it names both the value at stake and what causes it to triumph or fail.

## The sentence

A controlling idea has this shape:

> **{Value} {triumphs | fails} because {cause}.**

- **Value** — the story's core moral value, phrased as a continuum with a positive and negative pole: justice/injustice, love/hate, courage/cowardice, honesty/deception.
- **Triumphs or fails** — the ending's verdict. A positive ending argues the value triumphs; a negative ending argues it fails (or a counter-value wins).
- **Cause** — the protagonist's action or quality that *produces* the verdict. This is what makes the idea usable: every scene can be checked against whether the protagonist is movi

# Motif and Symbolism

A motif is a recurring concrete element — an object, image, phrase, or action — that accrues meaning across the story. Unlike theme (an idea), a motif is a *thing the reader can see*. This reference covers the structural mechanics: planting, varying, and paying off.

Readers forgive dragons but not armies that never eat. Work out what things cost, how goods move, and what power costs its users, then keep the numbers consistent.

# Maps and Routes

A story map is a graph before it is a picture: which places connect, how long the journey takes, and by what means. Record that graph in the location sections so the continuity scan can check travel against the timeline.

## Recording routes

Add a Routes block to a location's section in `./book/knowledge/locations.md`, one entry per direct connection:

```markdown
- **Routes:**
  - to: saltmarsh-fort — 9 hours coach
  - to: the-narrows — 4 hours boat
```

- `to` — the name of another location in `locations.md`.
- `hours` — travel time as a number (decimals allowed: `0.5` is thirty minutes).
- `mode` — free text: `on foot`, `horse`, `coach`, `river barge`, `airship`.

Routes are two-way unless the other location declares its own route back. Declare the return route only when it differs: against the current, uphill, or slower in a season (note the season in the location body).

## The continuity travel check

The continuity scan (`/buchbinder review`, `/buchbinder timeline`) uses routes together with scene dates, times, and locations, and the scene's characters and POV. When a character appears in two dated scenes at locations linked by routes, and the story time between the scenes is less than the fastest route (possibly through other places), it reports an error: the character could not have made the trip. A named time covers a span, and a scene with a date but no time spans its whole day. The gap is taken at its most generous reading, so only a journey impossible on every reading is an error. A character at two different places at the same exact time is an error even with no route between them.

To fix a finding:

1. Move the later scene's date or time later.
2. Change the route's mode and hours if a faster means exists in the story — and show that means on the page.
3. Remove the character from one scene's characters (list them as only referred to if they are not on the page).

# Naming Languages

Names carry a culture's sound. A few rules per culture make names feel related, keep cultures distinct from each other, and prevent accidental look-alikes that confuse readers.

## Phonology sketch

For each culture or language, write a short sketch in the `## [Social System]` section of `./book/knowledge/world-setting.md`, or in the culture section of a location or faction:

- **Sounds used:** consonants and vowels the language favours (`k, t, r, s, v, l; a, e, o`), and sounds it never uses (`no th, no w`)
- **Syllable shape:** `CV`, `CVC`, clusters allowed or not (`str-` yes, final `-ng` no)
- **Stress:** first syllable, penultimate, or last
- **Common endings:** `-ar`, `-ek`, `-issa` and what they mark (place, person, gender, rank)
- **Spelling conventions:** how sounds are written (`k` never `c`), apostrophes and accents (use sparingly; each one slows the reader)

Keep two cultures apart by changing at least two of: sound set, syllable shape, and endings.

# System Template

Use this structure for a `## [System Name]` section in `./book/knowledge/world-setting.md`. Systems represent structured aspects of the world: magic, politics, technology, religion, economy, etc.

```markdown
## {System Name}

- **Type:** {magic | political | technology | religion | economic | military | social | education | other}
- **Prevalence:** {universal | common | uncommon | rare | secret}

### Overview
What this system is and its role in the world. One paragraph summary.

### Rules & Limitations
How the system works. What it can and cannot do. Costs, constraints, and consequences. Be specific — well-defined limitations make systems compelling.

### History
How the system developed or was discovered. Key historical moments that shaped its current form.

### Practitioners
Who uses or participates in this system. Social status, requirements, training, organizations.

### Impact on Society
How this system shapes daily life, culture, politics, and conflict in the world. Ripple effects.
```

For any power, always answer the cost / limit / recovery triad (see `economy-logistics.md`). Systems do not take progressions — track how they change through the continuity state checks instead.
